course.title: French for Business
course.description: A CEFR B1 course in professional French: introduce yourself at work, run meetings, negotiate, and write polished business emails with confidence.

lessons.title: Professional introductions
lessons.grammar_note: In a professional setting French stays formal by default: use *vous*, address people as *Madame* or *Monsieur* without their surname, and wait for the other person to switch to *tu* before you do.

items.example: Permettez-moi de me présenter : Julien Marchand, du service commercial.

items.term: Je travaille dans le secteur de…
items.ipa: ʒə tʁa.vaj dɑ̃ lə sɛk.tœʁ də
items.example: Je travaille dans le secteur de la logistique depuis cinq ans.
Je suis responsable des relations avec nos clients européens.
Voici ma carte de visite ; n'hésitez pas à me contacter.
Ravi de faire votre connaissance, Madame Lefèvre.

items.translation: What field do you work in?
items.example: Et vous, dans quel domaine travaillez-vous exactement ?

sections.heading: When vous is expected
sections.text: In business, *vous* is the safe default with clients, suppliers, managers, and anyone you have just met. It marks respect and professional distance. Using *tu* too early can sound presumptuous, so let the more senior person or the host propose it: *On peut se tutoyer ?* Until then, stay with *vous*, even with colleagues you see every day.

sections.heading: The forms to master
sections.text: *Vous* takes the same verb ending in the present, the future, and the conditional: *Vous travaillez, vous travaillerez, vous travailleriez.* Its object and possessive forms are *vous* and *votre / vos*: *Je vous envoie votre devis et vos factures.* Reflexive verbs use *vous* too: *Comment vous appelez-vous ? Vous vous occupez de ce dossier ?*

sections.heading: Politeness that comes with it
sections.text: Formal register is more than a pronoun. Frame requests softly: *Pourriez-vous…?* rather than *Vous pouvez…?*, and open with *Excusez-moi de vous déranger.* Add *Madame* or *Monsieur* to soften a direct question: *Vous avez une minute, Monsieur ?* These small cushions matter far more in French than a simple *please* tacked on at the end.

sections.heading: Titles and names
sections.text: Address people as *Madame* or *Monsieur* alone — never followed by the surname in speech, unlike English. *Bonjour Madame* is correct; *Bonjour Madame Lefèvre* sounds oddly formal or even cold. Professional titles replace the name in some contexts: *Monsieur le Directeur, Madame la Présidente.* When in doubt, a plain *Madame / Monsieur* is always safe.

body.scenario: The coffee break at a professional conference in Paris. Approach someone you don't know, introduce yourself and your role, exchange a business card, and find one point in common that could lead to future contact.
body.persona: A busy but friendly sector professional who is happy to chat for a few minutes and appreciates a confident, polite opener
body.goal: Introduce yourself formally, say what you do, ask about the other person's field, and propose staying in touch — all using vous

lessons.title: Running a meeting
lessons.grammar_note: French meetings often use *on* for a collective *we*: *On commence ?* (Shall we start?), *On en reparle demain* (We'll come back to it tomorrow). It takes the *il/elle* verb form and feels warmer and less stiff than *nous*.

items.example: Le premier point à l'ordre du jour concerne le budget.

items.translation: to take stock / review where things stand
items.example: Avant de continuer, faisons le point sur le projet.

items.translation: to take the floor / start speaking
items.example: Est-ce que quelqu'un souhaite prendre la parole ?
Je vous enverrai le compte rendu de la réunion demain matin.

items.translation: to bring up / address a topic
items.example: Nous aborderons ce sujet à la prochaine réunion.

items.translation: let's get back to the point
items.example: Bon, revenons à nos moutons : le calendrier de livraison.

body.scenario: You are chairing your team's weekly project meeting by video call. Open the meeting, go through two agenda points, invite a quiet colleague to speak, keep a talkative one on topic, and close with the next steps and deadlines.
body.persona: A mixed team of French colleagues: one who dominates the discussion and one who stays silent unless invited to contribute
body.goal: Structure the meeting with agenda vocabulary, use the futur to assign next steps (Marie enverra le devis, on se reverra jeudi), and close politely on time

sections.heading: Conditionnel de politesse
sections.text: The conditional turns blunt demands into professional requests. Build it on the future stem plus imparfait endings: *vouloir → je voudrais*, *pouvoir → vous pourriez*, *aimer → j'aimerais*, *souhaiter → je souhaiterais*. Compare *Je veux votre réponse aujourd'hui* (abrupt) with *Je voudrais votre réponse aujourd'hui, si possible* (professional). *Pourriez-vous me confirmer le tarif ?* is the everyday workhorse of business French.

sections.heading: Le subjonctif in requests
sections.text: When you ask someone else to do something, French often needs the subjunctive after *que*. Trigger phrases include *il faudrait que*, *j'aimerais que*, *je voudrais que*: *Il faudrait que vous signiez le contrat avant vendredi. J'aimerais que nous soyons d'accord sur le prix.* Note the irregulars you cannot avoid: *que vous soyez* (être), *que vous ayez* (avoir), *que nous fassions* (faire).

sections.heading: Le futur for plans and commitments
sections.text: Use the simple future for firm professional commitments and scheduling: *Je vous enverrai le contrat lundi. Nous confirmerons la date cette semaine. L'équipe livrera le projet fin mars.* It sounds more reliable and formal than the near future (*je vais envoyer*), which fits casual speech. In writing especially, the futur simple is the register clients expect.

sections.heading: Putting it together
sections.text: A polished request often chains all three: a conditional to open, a subjunctive to specify, a future to commit. *Pourriez-vous vérifier le devis ? Il faudrait qu'il soit validé aujourd'hui, et je vous répondrai avant la fin de la journée.* This is the exact rhythm of professional French — soft opening, precise middle, confident close.

lessons.title: Negotiation & business email vocabulary
lessons.grammar_note: French business emails end with a fixed formula, not a casual *bye*. *Cordialement* is the reliable neutral sign-off; *Bien à vous* is warmer; the full *Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, mes salutations distinguées* is reserved for very formal letters.

items.example: Nous sommes prêts à faire une offre dès cette semaine.
Discutons des conditions de paiement avant de signer.
Je suis sûr que nous pouvons trouver un compromis.
Nous acceptons, sous réserve de votre accord sur le délai.
Vous trouverez le contrat en pièce jointe.

sections.heading: Subject line and greeting
sections.text: Start with a clear *Objet* (subject): *Objet : Demande de devis — projet logistique.* Open with the person's title, not their name: *Madame,* or *Monsieur,* on its own line, or *Madame, Monsieur,* when you don't know who will read it. Avoid *Cher / Chère* with people you don't know well — it is warmer than English *Dear* and can feel too familiar in a first contact.

sections.heading: Body: get to the point politely
sections.text: State your purpose in the first sentence with a set opener: *Je me permets de vous contacter au sujet de… / Suite à notre conversation téléphonique, je vous confirme…* Keep paragraphs short and requests conditional: *Pourriez-vous m'indiquer vos disponibilités ? Je vous serais reconnaissant de bien vouloir confirmer avant vendredi.* Reference attachments explicitly: *Vous trouverez notre proposition en pièce jointe.*

sections.heading: Closing formulas
sections.text: French sign-offs are graded by formality. Everyday professional email: *Cordialement,* or *Bien cordialement,* followed by your name. Slightly warmer: *Bien à vous,* Formal letters and first contact with senior people: *Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, mes salutations distinguées.* Never mix registers — a casual body with a grand closing looks odd.

sections.heading: A short model to imitate
sections.text: *Objet : Confirmation de rendez-vous. Madame, Je me permets de vous contacter afin de confirmer notre rendez-vous du 12 mars à 14 h. Pourriez-vous me préciser l'adresse exacte de vos bureaux ? Je vous en remercie par avance. Cordialement, Julien Marchand.* Notice the pattern: subject, greeting, purpose, polite request, thanks, sign-off — reusable for almost any business email.

body.scenario: A phone call with a client who finds your quote too high. Acknowledge their concern, defend your price with one clear argument, offer a compromise on either the price or the payment terms, and agree on the next step in writing.
body.persona: A polite but firm client who pushes for a discount and will only agree if you offer something concrete in return
body.goal: Negotiate using conditional requests (nous pourrions, il faudrait que), propose a real compromis, and close by confirming you will send a written devis

questions.prompt: Which is the most professional way to ask a client for confirmation?
options: Pourriez-vous me confirmer, s'il vous plaît ?
questions.explanation: The conditionnel de politesse *Pourriez-vous…?* plus *s'il vous plaît* is the standard polite business request; the others are too abrupt.

questions.prompt: Complete: « Il faudrait que vous ___ le contrat avant vendredi. »
questions.explanation: *Il faudrait que* triggers the subjunctive: *que vous signiez*. The indicative *signez* is wrong after this expression.

questions.prompt: In a business meeting, « l'ordre du jour » is…
questions.explanation: *L'ordre du jour* is the agenda — the list of points to be discussed. The written record afterwards is *le compte rendu*.

questions.prompt: Which sign-off best fits an everyday professional email?
questions.explanation: *Cordialement* is the neutral professional standard. *Bisous*, *À plus*, and *Salut* are informal and inappropriate for business.

questions.prompt: For a firm scheduling commitment to a client, which is most appropriate?
options: Je vais peut-être envoyer le contrat.
Je vous enverrai le contrat lundi.
questions.explanation: The futur simple *je vous enverrai* states a reliable commitment. The conditional *enverrais* would mean *would send*, and the others are vague or a command.

questions.prompt: « Nous acceptons, sous réserve de votre accord sur le délai. » This means the acceptance is…
options: conditional on their agreement about the deadline
questions.explanation: *Sous réserve de* means *subject to / provided that*, so the acceptance depends on their agreement on the deadline.
